newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Death in childbirth "biggest tragedy" in Africa, Asia.
newsitem.headline: Death in childbirth "biggest tragedy" in Africa, Asia.

text.p: A million women die each year in childbirth, most of them in Africa and southern Asia, with their numbers rising each year, according to an international group of physicians.

Calling maternal mortality the "biggest tragedy of our time," Dr. Daniel Weinstein, president of the World Society of Labour and Delivery, told reporters on Tuesday that "more people are dying in labour and delivery than all the dead in all the wars."
In an attempt to focus attention on the issue, the society has organised a conference in Marrakesh, Morocco, on March 8-14 for doctors, scientists, midwives and other health specialists.

Weinstein, chairman of the department of obstetrics and gynecology at the Hadassah Medical Centre in Jerusalem, plans to organise a team of health workers for a crash programme in one African country, not yet chosen, to show that deaths during childbirth can be appreciably reduced.

But he has had trouble raising the more than $500,000 needed for the Marrakesh conference from U.N. agencies or foundations. Only two countries, Switzerland and Norway, responded to an appeal for funds.
"One reason that the world is quiet is that we don't hear any noise from Africa, from Asia," he said. "They are dying in silence. And the silence has put the world to sleep."

In Somalia, he said, 1 of every 7 women dies in childbirth; in the Ivory Coast it is 1 of every 14, in Bolivia 1 out of every 26 women and in Morocco 1 out of every 33. In comparison, 1 of every 3,500 women dies in childbirth in the United States and in Israel the figure is 1 out of every 4,000.

UNICEF, the U.N. Children's Fund, which will be sending representatives to the conference, in its annual report estimated nearly 600,000 deaths in childbirth in 1990. It concluded that "there is no evidence that significant progress has been made."

Most of these deaths are from obstetric causes: haemorrhage, sepsis, obstructed labour and unsafe abortions as well as some medical conditions. But the agency found that training of lay health care workers in isolation from a general health care system had little impact.
Weinstein attributed half the deaths to a lack of family planning that resulted in unwanted pregnancies and self-induced lethal abortions.
Many of the women, he said, were far too young to bear a child, their bodies not yet having reached full growth.
"If just family planning was introduced properly, the number of deaths will drop by half," he said.
